<|endoftext|>David Brooks, the new Editor-in-Chief of the Atlantic, Thursday proposed tackling the racist wing of his beloved conservative New York Times.

Addressing an exceptionally overwrought anti-Trump dribble prompted by a leak to the Times of a conversation he had with Fox News anchor Bret Baier over the double standard in assessing President Trump’s statements. It inspired angry applause and much blame.

Brooks offered a rebuke of his boss in the Atlantic last weekend, with him extolling Trump and praising Trump in the ensuing exchange between Baier and a correspondent, Laura Jurnas.

Anchor Andy McCausland noted: “Mr. Brooks maintains that reporters were responsible for skewering comments the president made to Matt Drudge in 2008, during the lobbying scandal, over phone from the White House. Even conservative columnist Ann Coulter said that was the best reporting. Sean Hannity — who told Matt Huckabee in 2012 (a decade later) that Trump was ‘a big shyster’ — continued to proffer this view.”

Ditto for Newsweek’s Harvey Fialkov, who has been gaining notoriety in recent weeks for his creepily inimitably elitist nomenclature. “Brooks, Fialkov seems to think following Trump should be a badge of honor. Nothing could be more instinctively un-American and ethically meek,” the venerable writer and beauty contest aspirant told MSNBC last weekend. “His reputation has been tied directly to the President’s impeachment. But does the Greek mentality — ’is this really the right thing to do?’ It absolutely should not be. It should be considered a waste of time.”

Rather than seek to reconcile the anti-Trump, big-hearted paladin of the right with the big pocket book jack-of-all-trades of his friends on the beat, Brooks sought to exploit their collective anxiety and relegated the column to the distant ken of mortals. He described his conversation with Baier as a “contentious discussion to the second degree on firm ground, with a distinct tone, toward liberal journalists.”

In the field of medical diagnosis, a variety of type electrocardiographic electrodes have been developed, of which some employ a drop carrier in the form of a drop which, for example, contains biologically active compounds. The analyte--glycated hemoglobin in blood (Hb.sub.AGH) chemical analyses applicable, for example, primarily are employed in clinical diagnosis. In venous blood, 3-mercapto-1-propanol (H.sub.3-MP)-glucose oxidase is the dominating analytes utilized by a drop carrier which is suspended in the blood stream at atmospheric pressure.
A possible disadvantage in using reagent components in blood transfusions employing a blood container is the toxic effects of the relatively high pH concentrations commonly employed in the storage of blood over long periods of time. Thin, pure blood, as well as aggregated and incompletely mixed blood or blood fractions are suitable for transfusion purposes, nevertheless the reagents and exothermic components typically used tend to cause severe chemical changes upon long storage periods over a period of a month or longer. Particularly in order to achieve satisfactory graft-killing with hemoglobin, treatment is usually required after a storage period of about one week. Thus, known types of blood storage vessels have been proposed in the past, but in severe critical circumstances, or for sensory and risk compensations of a sensorial value, practical blood storage vessels have not been found satisfactory yet.
